The surveillance buildout
AI has turned cameras from passive recorders into active identifiers. A Deloitte survey found cities deploying facial recognition and biometrics (84%), in-car and body cameras (55%), and drones and aerial surveillance (46%) for public safety. Market-research projections are steep — one puts AI in predictive policing at about $3.4 billion in 2024 rising to roughly $157 billion by 2034, a ~46.7% compound annual rate — but the projection is unattributed in the material we found and implies 46-fold growth in a decade, so treat it as a sign of vendor enthusiasm rather than a forecast. A December 2024 US Department of Justice report grouped law-enforcement AI into four uses — identification and surveillance, forensic analytics, predictive policing, and risk assessment.
The corporate face database
Much of the infrastructure is private. Clearview AI assembled a database of more than 50 billion facial images by scraping social media and the open web without consent, then sold face-matching access to law-enforcement and government clients. The model has drawn fines and bans in several countries for breaching privacy law. In the US, an Illinois biometric-privacy class action produced an unusual settlement in 2025: instead of cash, class members received a 23% stake in the company, valued at about $51.75 million. On 13 July 2026 the Seventh Circuit vacated its approval, finding the nationwide class lacked independent representation, and sent the case back. The database size of 50+ billion images (60+ billion in later reports) is Clearview's own figure. The case illustrates the core problem: once your face is online, it can be enrolled in an identification system you never agreed to.
“Once your face is online, it can be enrolled in an identification system you never agreed to.”
Predictive policing and its bias
Predictive systems forecast where crime will occur or who is “high risk,” then direct patrols accordingly. Because they learn from historical arrest data, they tend to send more police to already over-policed neighborhoods, generating more arrests that confirm the prediction — a feedback loop. Combined with facial recognition’s higher error rates for darker-skinned faces, the result can be discriminatory enforcement dressed up as objective analytics, contradicting principles like the presumption of innocence and equal protection.
Deployment without a statute
The June version of this page set the buildout against an emerging legal pushback. The record since points to a third pattern that matters more in democracies: surveillance capability expanding ahead of the law, or around it.
United Kingdom: fifty vans, no dedicated law
On 26 January 2026 the Home Office's policing white paper proposed funding 40 more live-facial-recognition vans on top of the 10 already in use — about 50 in all, aimed at every force in England and Wales — plus more than £26 million for a national facial-recognition system. Deployment is already widening: Norfolk police reportedly scanned more than 50,000 faces in Norwich in March 2026 with borrowed vans, and recent reporting puts one force's cumulative scans above 400,000. The white paper promises a bespoke legal framework; none has been enacted. Live facial recognition in the UK runs on general policing powers and guidance, and Big Brother Watch has said it will appeal a recent ruling that left the expansion unrestrained (a single report; we have not seen the judgment).
United States: identification in the field
ICE's Mobile Fortify, first reported in June 2025, lets agents photograph a person and match the face against federal biometric records from a phone, returning possible identities on the spot. DHS's 2025 AI use-case inventory, published in January 2026, confirmed it runs on NEC face-matching technology. Reporting based on internal records puts use at roughly 100,000 times; a privacy assessment reportedly sets retention at 15 years, including photos that match no one. A DHS Inspector General audit had warned in February 2025 that reliance on facial recognition risked misidentification, and senators have demanded the app be withdrawn. There is no warrant requirement for its use.
Cities: bans that did not hold
Several US cities restrict police facial recognition. New Orleans is the cautionary case. A 2022 ordinance allowed it only for documented investigations of violent crime and barred continuous live monitoring. In May 2025 the Washington Post reported that police had nevertheless received real-time face-match alerts for about two years from Project NOLA, a private network of more than 5,000 cameras, over 200 of them running face recognition. The alerts were paused on 8 April 2025 after inquiries; whether use resumed is disputed and unconfirmed.
The common thread is that the constraint in each case was not the technology but the absence or circumvention of a rule. That is the more useful frame for readers in democracies than the authoritarian end of the spectrum, which follows.
The authoritarian end — and the pushback
At the far end, AI surveillance becomes a tool of control: mass facial-recognition networks, social-scoring pilots, and the export of surveillance platforms to states that use them to track dissidents. The counterweight is emerging in law: the EU AI Act has, since 2 February 2025, prohibited real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces for law enforcement except in narrowly defined cases such as searching for victims or preventing an imminent threat, and bans untargeted scraping of facial images to build recognition databases — the Clearview model — outright, several US cities have banned government facial recognition, and courts are scrutinizing scraped-image databases. The throughline of this series applies here too — the technology is only as accountable as the humans and rules governing its use.

Frequently asked
How widespread is AI surveillance?
Very, and growing. A Deloitte survey found around 84% of cities using facial recognition or biometrics for public safety; the UK plans to expand police live-facial-recognition vans from 10 to about 50; ICE's field face-matching app has reportedly been used around 100,000 times; and Clearview AI says its database holds more than 50 billion scraped facial images.
Why is predictive policing controversial?
It learns from biased historical data, which can send more police to already over-policed areas in a self-reinforcing loop, and it pairs with facial recognition that misidentifies minorities more often — raising due-process, privacy, and equal-protection concerns.
Is live facial recognition legal in the UK?
It is used under general policing powers and guidance rather than a dedicated law. The January 2026 policing white paper proposed expanding police live-facial-recognition vans from 10 to about 50 and promised a bespoke legal framework, which has not been enacted.
What is ICE's Mobile Fortify app?
A phone app, first reported in June 2025, that lets immigration agents photograph a person and match their face against federal biometric records in the field. It runs on NEC technology, has reportedly been used about 100,000 times, and reportedly retains images for 15 years, including those that match no one.
Does the EU ban facial recognition?
Partly. Since 2 February 2025 the EU AI Act has prohibited real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces for law enforcement except in narrowly defined cases, and has banned untargeted scraping of facial images to build recognition databases.

=== PAGE 546 | Copyright and AI: Who Owns the Rights? | https://report-ai.org/reports/dark-side-of-ai/ai-copyright-who-owns-the-rights/ | modified 2026-10-29 | type page
Home / Reports / The Dark Side of AI / Copyright & AIDark Side of AI · Report
COPYRIGHT AND AI: WHO OWNS THE RIGHTS?
Generative AI has forced two unsettled questions to the center of copyright law: who owns what AI makes, and who owns what AI learned from. So far the answer for purely machine-made work is “no one,” while the training fight plays out in dozens of lawsuits worth billions.
By Report AI·Updated Oct 29, 2026·10 min read
Key takeaways
→AI output isn’t automatically yours: the US Copyright Office ruled in 2025 that works made entirely by AI are not copyrightable — human authorship is required. (US Copyright Office)
→Prompts alone aren’t enough: one artist’s 600+ prompts still failed to earn copyright; only human-made contributions are protectable. (Review Board)
→The training fight is huge: the New York Times is suing OpenAI for billions; Anthropic settled an authors’ class action for $1.5 billion — after a judge held that training was fair use, but keeping a library of pirated books was not. (Bartz v. Anthropic, N.D. Cal.)
→The first appeal has been decided: on 29 September 2026 the Third Circuit rejected fair use in Thomson Reuters v. Ross — for a non-generative legal-search tool, expressly leaving generative AI open. (3d Cir.)
→The US government is arguing both sides: the Copyright Office says training is fair use only “in some circumstances”; the Justice Department intervened on 2 September 2026 to back OpenAI against the New York Times. (USCO; DOJ)
→The decisive case is close: the consolidated NYT v. OpenAI litigation (MDL 3143) is at summary judgment on fair use. (S.D.N.Y.)
$1.5B
Anthropic’s settlement with authors over pirated training books
1st
US appeals ruling on AI training: fair use rejected, 29 Sept 2026 · 3d Cir.
600+
prompts that still weren’t enough to earn copyright
What changed · two corrections
Reviewed 28 Oct 2026 · FAQ wording corrected 29 Oct · previously 20 Jun 2026 · next review 28 Nov 2026
First review since publication. Two statements on the June page were wrong when they were written, and the field has since produced its first appellate ruling.
 |   | Was (Jun 2026) | Now
 | Anthropic ruling | “ingesting … pirated books for commercial training went well beyond fair use” | Corrected. The judge held training was fair use; acquiring and keeping a pirated library was not
 | Copyright Office training report | “still pending” | Corrected. A pre-publication Part 3 was released on 9 May 2025; only the final version is outstanding
 | Appellate law | none | Third Circuit, Thomson Reuters v. Ross, 29 Sept 2026: fair use rejected (non-generative)
 | Thaler | D.C. Circuit ruling | Supreme Court denied review, 2 Mar 2026
 | Case count | “51” as headline tile | dated to Oct 2025; no reliable current count — trackers disagree
Why the first correction matters. It reversed the lesson. A reader of the June page would have taken away that training on books is not fair use. The court in Bartz v. Anthropic said close to the opposite: training was “exceedingly transformative”, and the liability came from how the books were obtained and stored. That is the distinction the whole field now turns on, and we had it backwards. The Copyright Office error was a fact we could have checked. Confidence: MEDIUM — court and Copyright Office sites are not reachable from our environment; detail rests on consistent law-firm analyses.
Who owns what AI makes?
In its January 2025 report, the US Copyright Office reaffirmed that human authorship is the bedrock of copyright — so a work generated entirely by AI cannot be registered, and no one owns an exclusive right to it. Crucially, the Office concluded that “prompts alone do not provide sufficient human control” to make a user the author of the output. This was tested by Jason Allen’s award-winning image Théâtre D’opéra Spatial, made with 600+ Midjourney prompts: registration was refused for the AI-generated elements, though his manual Photoshop edits could qualify. The federal courts agree on the core point — in Thaler v. Perlmutter, the D.C. Circuit confirmed an AI cannot be the legal author, and on 2 March 2026 the Supreme Court declined to hear the appeal — not a ruling on the merits, but it leaves the human-authorship requirement in place. Where a human meaningfully shapes a work, that person owns their contribution; the machine-made parts fall into a copyright gap.
“Prompts alone do not provide sufficient human control to make a user the author of AI output.”
Who owns what AI learned from?
The bigger money is in the input. Model makers trained on vast troves of copyrighted text and images, and rights-holders are suing. The New York Times sued OpenAI and Microsoft (filed December 2023), seeking billions and alleging its articles were copied to build competing products. Anthropic agreed to a roughly $1.5 billion settlement in Bartz v. Anthropic — but the ruling that led there is often misreported, including in an earlier version of this page. In June 2025 Judge William Alsup held that training Claude on copyrighted books was fair use, calling it “exceedingly transformative”, and that scanning lawfully purchased print books was fair use too. What he refused to excuse was downloading millions of pirated books and keeping them as a permanent central library. That issue was sent to trial, the class was certified, and the settlement followed. The liability came from acquisition and storage, not from learning. Getty Images, record labels, and authors including a New York Times investigative reporter have brought parallel claims against Stability AI, Suno, xAI, Meta, Google, and others.
The fair-use battleground
The central legal question — is training on copyrighted work “fair use”? — remains unresolved. In October 2025 one tracker counted 51 copyright suits against AI companies; filings have continued since — publishers and authors against Google in July 2026, USA Today against OpenAI and Microsoft on 8 October, new claims against Suno — and trackers no longer agree on a total, so we do not give one. The district-court rulings split along a now-familiar line: in Bartz v. Anthropic and Kadrey v. Meta (both June 2025) judges found training on books to be fair use, while piracy-related claims survived; in Thomson Reuters v. Ross (February 2025) the court found no fair use for a non-generative tool built on Westlaw headnotes.
The first appeal
On 29 September 2026 the Third Circuit affirmed Thomson Reuters v. Ross, the first US appellate decision on whether copying works to train an AI system is fair use. It held that it was not. Two qualifications matter more than the headline. Ross built a legal-search tool that returned existing material, not a generative model, and the court reserved the generative question. And one circuit's ruling binds only that circuit. Anyone describing training-as-fair-use as settled — either way — is describing district courts.
The government on both sides
The US Copyright Office released a pre-publication version of Part 3 of its AI report, on training, on 9 May 2025. It concluded that training on copyrighted works “likely qualifies as fair use in some circumstances, but not in others”, and gave unusual weight to market dilution — harm from a flood of AI output competing with human work, even where no individual work is copied. The Register of Copyrights, Shira Perlmutter, was removed the next day; an appeals court reinstated her in September 2025, and on 30 June 2026 the Supreme Court declined to stay that order. The final version of Part 3 has not been published.
Meanwhile, on 2 September 2026 the Justice Department intervened in the consolidated New York Times litigation against OpenAI and Microsoft (MDL 3143) in support of OpenAI's fair-use position. So the federal government's copyright agency says training is sometimes infringing, while its litigators argue on behalf of one of the largest trainers. That case is now at summary judgment on fair use, and is the most likely next landmark. Until courts or Congress settle it, the rules are being written case by case.
What it means for creators and businesses
The practical takeaways are sharp. If your team generates a logo, image, or article purely from a prompt, you likely cannot claim exclusive copyright in it — a competitor may be free to reuse it. To secure rights, keep a human meaningfully in the creative loop and document that contribution. And on the input side, businesses that build on models trained from unlicensed data inherit legal uncertainty until the courts rule. The throughline of this series holds: AI accelerates creation, but ownership and accountability still attach to humans.

Corrections in this review. The June version mischaracterised the Bartz ruling as finding that training on pirated books exceeded fair use; the court held training was fair use and the pirated library was not. It also described the Copyright Office's training report as pending when a pre-publication version had been public since May 2025. Both are corrected above. No current total of AI copyright suits is given because trackers disagree. This page is not legal advice. Cadence: CRITICAL (monthly) while NYT v. OpenAI is at summary judgment.
Frequently asked
Can you copyright AI-generated art or writing?
Not if it is generated entirely by AI. The US Copyright Office requires human authorship, and ruled in 2025 that prompts alone are not enough. Only the human-created portions of a mixed human-AI work can be copyrighted, assessed case by case.
Who owns the output of an AI tool I used?
If a human meaningfully shaped the work, that person owns their contribution; purely machine-generated elements generally aren’t protected by copyright at all. A provider’s terms of service may grant you usage rights, but that is different from owning an enforceable copyright.
Is training AI on copyrighted work legal?
It’s unresolved. Dozens of lawsuits are testing whether training is fair use; early rulings are split and often hinge on whether the data was lawfully obtained. In Bartz v. Anthropic the judge held that training on books was fair use, but that downloading and keeping a library of pirated copies was not; the case then settled for about $1.5 billion. On 29 September 2026 the Third Circuit issued the first appellate ruling, rejecting fair use in Thomson Reuters v. Ross — for a non-generative tool, with the generative question left open.
What did the Anthropic copyright case actually decide?
In June 2025 Judge William Alsup held that training Claude on copyrighted books was fair use and that scanning lawfully bought print books was fair use, but that acquiring millions of pirated books and keeping them in a permanent library was not. That piracy issue was headed to trial when Anthropic settled the authors' class action for about $1.5 billion. It is easy to misread as a finding that AI training itself is not fair use; an earlier version of this page made that mistake.
What does the US government say about AI training and copyright?
Two different things. The Copyright Office's pre-publication report of May 2025 concluded that training is likely fair use in some circumstances but not others, with particular concern for market dilution. In September 2026 the Justice Department intervened in the New York Times litigation in support of OpenAI's fair-use position. The Copyright Office's final report has not been published.

=== PAGE 545 | AI Slop: The Synthetic Flood Polluting the Internet | https://report-ai.org/reports/dark-side-of-ai/ai-slop-content-pollution-internet/ | modified 2026-10-29 | type page
Home / Reports / The Dark Side of AI / AI Slop
Dark Side of AI · Report
AI SLOP: THE SYNTHETIC FLOOD POLLUTING THE INTERNET
The web is filling with machine-made filler. Generative AI has made it almost free to produce text, images, and audio at infinite scale — and the result is “AI slop”: low-quality synthetic content that crowds out human work, games search engines, fuels a new fake-news industry, and erodes the line between real and fake. The pollution is now measurable.
By Report AI·Updated Oct 29, 2026·10 min read
Key takeaways
→AI is in most new pages, and writes about half of new articles: 74.2% of newly published pages contained some AI-generated content (Ahrefs, Apr 2025); articles written primarily by AI have held near 50% for five quarters. (Ahrefs; Graphite, Q1 2026)
→A new fake-news industry: NewsGuard now tracks 3,749 AI content-farm news sites across 16 languages — nearly three times the 2025 count of 1,271 this page previously used. (NewsGuard, Jun 2026)
→It is monetized: blue-chip brand ads routinely run on AI content farms publishing fabricated stories.
→The trust cost: in NewsGuard's monthly audits, leading chatbots repeated false news claims 18% of the time in August 2024, 35% in August 2025 and 28.8% in January 2026. (NewsGuard AI False Claims Monitor)
→Made at scale, barely consumed: AI tracks passed 50% of Deezer's daily uploads in June 2026 — but account for only 1–3% of streams. (Deezer, Jul 2026)

Reviewed 29 Oct 2026 · previously 20 Jun 2026 · next review 29 Jan 2027
First review since publication. Two of the June page's four headline figures were misattributed or untraceable, a third had nearly tripled, and the new data adds a twist the page did not have: AI content is being produced in enormous volume but consumed far less than its volume suggests.

Confidence. MEDIUM. The figures are publishers' own measurements (Ahrefs, Graphite, NewsGuard, Deezer) using their own detectors and definitions; their sites are not reachable from our research environment, so we rely on consistent reporting of them. AI-detection methods carry error rates of their own.
The flood
The tipping point has arrived. In April 2025, Ahrefs analyzed 900,000 newly published English-language pages and found 74.2% contained AI-generated content; a separate study by the SEO firm Graphite, sampling articles from Common Crawl, estimated that articles written primarily by AI first outnumbered human-written ones in November 2024. Graphite's follow-up, with data through the first quarter of 2026, found the share has since levelled off near 50% — 50.9% in the fourth quarter of 2025, 49.9% in the first quarter of 2026 — rather than continuing to climb. The two figures measure different things: Ahrefs counts any AI content in a page; Graphite counts articles that are mainly machine-written. Most of this is not deliberate disinformation — it is cheap filler built to capture search traffic and ad clicks. But at this volume it degrades search results, buries original reporting, and risks future models training on the synthetic exhaust of earlier ones.
“Machines now write about half of new articles — and the share has stopped rising.”
The fake-news economy
Slop shades into something worse when it wears the costume of journalism. NewsGuard has identified 3,749 AI content-farm news and information sites across 16 languages as of June 2026 — up from the 1,271 it counted in 2025 and quoted here previously — using criteria that require both substantial AI-produced content and evidence of publication without meaningful human oversight. Independent researchers counting with looser criteria report far more; one has catalogued around 15,000 in French alone, a figure not comparable with NewsGuard's. Many churn out fabricated stories with minimal human oversight. These farms are funded by programmatic advertising: in one 2025 case, a fabricated story about Coca-Cola and the Super Bowl ran alongside ads from major brands including Expedia, AT&T, and GoDaddy — the advertisers unaware their budgets were bankrolling fake news.
Music, books, and reviews
The flood spans every medium. A fully AI-generated “band,” the Velvet Sundown, racked up more than a million Spotify plays in mid-2025 before its synthetic origins were widely noticed; Spotify says it removed 75 million spam tracks over the prior year. Online stores have filled with AI-written books and fake reviews, making it harder for readers and shoppers to tell authentic work from machine output.
Produced at scale, barely consumed
The clearest single dataset on AI slop now comes from music, and it complicates the flood narrative in a useful way. Deezer, which runs its own AI-detection tool on uploads, reported that AI-generated tracks rose from about 10% of daily uploads in January 2025 to 44% in April 2026 — some 75,000 a day — and passed 50% in June 2026. Yet Deezer says those tracks account for only 1–3% of total streams.
That gap is the most important number on this page. It suggests the supply flood is real but the attention flood is, so far, much smaller: people are not, in the main, choosing to listen to AI tracks. The same pattern appears in text, where Graphite found the AI share of new articles levelling off near half rather than continuing to rise. The economic harm of slop is therefore less about displacing what people consume than about raising the cost of finding it — for listeners, readers, search engines and the platforms that have to filter it. These are one platform's figures from its own detector, not a market-wide measure.
The cost to trust
The deepest damage is to the information commons. When most new content is synthetic and a meaningful share is wrong — NewsGuard’s monthly audits found leading chatbots repeating false news claims 18% of the time in August 2024, 35% in August 2025 and 28.8% in January 2026, a rise NewsGuard attributes largely to chatbots now answering questions they once declined, drawing on a web increasingly seeded with falsehoods — the baseline assumption that online content is human and checkable breaks down. The defenses are the same ones surfacing across this series: provenance and labeling (C2PA), AI-content detection, and platforms enforcing quality, not just volume.

Frequently asked
How much of the internet is now AI-generated?
It depends on the measure. A 2025 Ahrefs analysis of 900,000 new pages found 74.2% contained some AI-generated content, ranging from lightly edited to fully synthetic. For articles written primarily by AI, Graphite estimates the share at about half, roughly stable since late 2024 (49.9% in the first quarter of 2026).
How many AI-generated fake news sites are there?
NewsGuard tracked 3,749 AI content-farm news and information sites across 16 languages as of June 2026, using strict criteria that require evidence of publication without meaningful human oversight. Counts using looser definitions are much higher.
Do people actually consume AI slop?
Much less than it is produced. On Deezer, AI-generated tracks passed half of daily uploads in June 2026 but account for only 1 to 3 percent of streams. The harm is less that people choose AI content than that it raises the cost of finding human work.
How often do AI chatbots repeat false news?
In NewsGuard's monthly audits, leading chatbots repeated false claims 18% of the time in August 2024, 35% in August 2025 and 28.8% in January 2026.
What is “AI slop”?
AI slop is low-quality, mass-produced synthetic content — articles, images, audio, reviews — generated to capture clicks or ad revenue rather than inform. At scale it pollutes search results, funds fake-news sites, and erodes trust in online information.

=== PAGE 544 | Algorithmic Bias: When AI Discriminates at Scale | https://report-ai.org/reports/dark-side-of-ai/ai-algorithmic-bias-discrimination/ | modified 2026-10-29 | type page
Home / Reports / The Dark Side of AI / Algorithmic Bias
 Dark Side of AI · Report
 ALGORITHMIC BIAS: WHEN AI DISCRIMINATES AT SCALE
 AI increasingly decides who gets arrested, hired, treated, or paroled — and the evidence shows it often decides unequally. Trained on historical data that encodes decades of human bias, algorithmic systems have produced wrongful arrests, discriminatory hiring screens, and unequal medical care, frequently against the people least equipped to contest a machine’s verdict.
 By Report AI·
 Updated Oct 29, 2026·
 10 min read
 Key takeaways
 →Facial recognition fails unevenly: MIT found error rates up to ~34 percentage points higher for darker-skinned women, and misidentifications have led to wrongful arrests. (MIT Gender Shades)
 →Hiring under scrutiny: the age-discrimination collective action against Workday’s AI screening, certified in 2025, was widened in March 2026 to include its HiredScore AI features; a class-certification hearing is set for March 2027. No court has found Workday liable. (Mobley v. Workday, N.D. Cal.)
 →Justice: ProPublica found the COMPAS risk tool flagged Black defendants as future criminals at nearly twice the rate of white defendants. (ProPublica)
 →In the US, governance retreated: federal agencies were told in April 2025 to deprioritise disparate-impact enforcement, and in May 2026 Colorado repealed its first-in-the-nation AI anti-discrimination duty before it ever took effect. (EO 14281; SB 26-189)
 →Elsewhere it slipped or held: the EU's high-risk AI obligations were pushed to December 2027; South Korea's AI Framework Act has been in force since January 2026. (EU Digital Omnibus)
 →Courts are doing the work regulators stepped back from: in the US, the live accountability route for biased AI is now litigation under existing civil-rights law.

 What changed
 Reviewed 29 Oct 2026 · previously 20 Jun 2026 · next review 29 Jan 2027
 First review since publication. The evidence of bias on this page — Gender Shades, COMPAS, the Science health-algorithm study — is unchanged and still stands. What changed is the direction of the response. The June page described governance tightening; across the US and EU, most of it has loosened or slipped.
 |   | Was (Jun 2026) | Now (29 Oct 2026)
 | Colorado AI Act | not covered | repealed and replaced (SB 26-189, 14 May 2026); anti-discrimination duty removed; new law from 1 Jan 2027
 | US federal posture | “agencies … testing civil-rights law” | EO 14281 directs agencies to deprioritise disparate-impact enforcement

 | Study dates | undated in tiles | dated (2016, 2018, 2019)
 Also fixed: two broken internal links. Confidence: MEDIUM for new legal material; legislature and court sites are not reachable from our research environment, so detail rests on consistent law-firm analyses.
 When the camera misidentifies
 MIT’s Gender Shades project exposed how unevenly facial recognition performs: leading commercial systems from Amazon, IBM, and Microsoft misclassified darker-skinned women far more often than lighter-skinned men, with some missing roughly a third of darker female faces. In the real world, those errors put people in handcuffs — at least eight Americans, nearly all of them Black, have been wrongfully arrested after a face-matching system pointed police at the wrong person (a count compiled from public reporting as of early 2025; we have not found an updated tally). Gender Shades dates from 2018, and commercial systems have improved since — but the arrests happened with deployed systems, which is the point. The technology is most error-prone precisely for the groups already over-policed.
 Hiring, lending, and healthcare
 Bias scales fastest where AI screens people at volume. In May 2025 a federal court in California let a nationwide collective action proceed alleging Workday’s AI screening disadvantaged applicants over 40. It has since grown rather than faded: notice went out in early 2026, a March 2026 ruling rejected Workday's argument that the age-discrimination statute does not protect job applicants and extended the collective to people screened with its HiredScore features, and a class-certification hearing is set for March 2027. No liability has been found. The case echoes Amazon’s earlier, scrapped recruiting tool that penalized résumés containing the word “women’s.” In healthcare, a widely used risk algorithm studied in Science systematically under-referred Black patients for extra care; correcting the bias would have more than doubled the share of Black patients flagged for help. The pattern: the model looks neutral, but the training data is not.
 "The model looks neutral, but the training data is not — bias scales fastest where AI screens people at volume."
 Justice by algorithm
 Risk-scoring tools now inform bail, sentencing, and parole. ProPublica’s investigation of COMPAS found it labeled Black defendants who did not reoffend as “high risk” at nearly twice the rate of comparable white defendants, while white defendants who did reoffend were more often rated low risk. Because such scores carry an air of objectivity, they can entrench discrimination while making it harder to challenge.
 The governance response
 The June version of this page said regulators were “beginning to treat fairness as a requirement, not an aspiration.” Four months later the honest description is the reverse in most of the places that matter.
 United States: a deliberate retreat
 In April 2025 Executive Order 14281, “Restoring Equality of Opportunity and Meritocracy”, directed federal agencies to abolish or deprioritise enforcement of disparate-impact liability — the legal theory under which a system can be discriminatory in effect without discriminatory intent. For algorithmic bias that is the theory that matters most, because models rarely intend anything; their harm shows up in outcomes.
 The state that went furthest then stepped back. Colorado's AI Act of 2024, the first US law to impose a duty of reasonable care against algorithmic discrimination, was delayed to June 2026 and then repealed and replaced before it ever took effect: SB 26-189, signed on 14 May 2026, substitutes a narrower transparency and consumer-rights framework from 1 January 2027, and eliminates the discrimination duty, deployer risk-management programmes and annual impact assessments. By then enforcement of the original law had already been stayed by a federal court on 27 April 2026, in a constitutional challenge brought by an AI developer and backed by the Justice Department.
 European Union: the classification stands, the obligations wait
 The EU AI Act still classes AI used in hiring, credit, education and access to public services as “high-risk”. But the Digital Omnibus, in force since 27 July 2026, postponed the obligations attached to that label to 2 December 2027 for most such systems. Until then, the bias-relevant duties of the Act — data governance, testing, documentation — do not yet bite.
 Where it held
 South Korea's AI Framework Act has been in force since January 2026 and requires measures against discrimination in high-impact AI, including healthcare and public services. And in the US, the accountability that regulators stepped back from is being pursued through the courts under existing law — Mobley v. Workday is the leading example.
 The upshot for anyone deploying AI in consequential decisions: in the US the risk has not gone away, it has moved from regulatory compliance to litigation, which is less predictable and arrives after the harm rather than before it. The throughline: when AI makes a high-stakes call, someone must remain accountable for auditing it and for the people it gets wrong.
 Frequently asked
 Is AI really biased, or is that overstated?
It is well documented. Peer-reviewed studies and investigations have found measurable bias in facial recognition, healthcare risk scoring, criminal-justice tools, and hiring systems — typically because the models learn from historical data that reflects past discrimination.
 Have people been harmed by biased AI?
Yes. At least eight Americans — nearly all Black — have been wrongfully arrested after facial-recognition misidentifications, and biased risk and healthcare algorithms have affected bail decisions and access to care for large populations.
 Is there a US law against algorithmic discrimination?
Not a dedicated federal one, and the leading state law was withdrawn. Colorado's 2024 AI Act imposed a duty of care against algorithmic discrimination, but it was repealed and replaced by SB 26-189 in May 2026 before taking effect, with a narrower transparency law from January 2027. Existing civil-rights and employment laws still apply, and are being tested in court.
 What is the Workday AI hiring lawsuit?
Mobley v. Workday is a nationwide collective action alleging Workday's AI screening disadvantaged job applicants aged 40 and over. A court allowed it to proceed in May 2025, extended it in March 2026 to include Workday's HiredScore features, and set a class-certification hearing for March 2027. No liability has been found.
 Does the EU AI Act stop biased AI?
Not yet. It classes AI in hiring, credit and public services as high-risk, but the 2026 Digital Omnibus postponed the obligations attached to that classification to December 2027 for most systems.
 Methodology & sources
 The evidence of bias on this page comes from peer-reviewed or investigative studies that are now several years old — Gender Shades (2018), ProPublica's COMPAS analysis (2016), Obermeyer et al. in Science (2019) — and they are dated accordingly. They remain the reference studies; newer systems may perform differently, and we have not found comparable independent audits that supersede them. The wrongful-arrest count is a compilation from public reporting as of early 2025.
 Legal and policy material — EO 14281, Colorado SB 24-205 and SB 26-189, the EU Digital Omnibus, Mobley v. Workday — rests on consistent analyses by multiple law firms; legislature, court and EUR-Lex sites are not reachable from our research environment. Accounts of the Workday case's procedural history differ in detail, and we give the version most sources share. New material is rated MEDIUM. Cadence: STANDARD (quarterly). === PAGE 543 | AI Companions and the Mental-Health Reckoning | https://report-ai.org/reports/dark-side-of-ai/ai-companion-chatbots-mental-health-harms/ | modified 2026-10-29 | type page

 Dark Side of AI · Report
 AI COMPANIONS AND THE MENTAL-HEALTH RECKONING
 As AI chatbots become companions — confidants, romantic partners, even stand-in therapists — a darker pattern has surfaced: vulnerable users, especially teenagers, forming deep dependencies on systems built with few guardrails. A wave of lawsuits, including one over the suicide of a 14-year-old, has turned AI companion harm into the most consequential consumer-safety story in AI.
 By Report AI·
 Updated Oct 28, 2026·
 11 min read
 Key takeaways
 →The defendant no longer exists as a going concern. Character.AI and Google settled the Setzer suit in January 2026. On 12 October 2026 Character.AI filed for Chapter 11, with Disney the lead bidder for its intellectual property. (Fortune; Deadline)
 →The scale of distress: in October 2025 OpenAI disclosed that roughly 1.2 million of its then ~800 million weekly ChatGPT users discussed suicide each week. We have found no update since, so the figure stays as a dated 2025 reading. (OpenAI, Oct 2025)
 →The harm pattern: suits allege chatbots manipulated and isolated teens, engaged in sexual conversations, and lacked crisis safeguards. (court filings)
 →Regulation arrived fast. California's SB 243 took effect 1 January 2026; Idaho, Oregon and Washington followed; and New York's Kids Chatbot Safety Act was signed on 28 October 2026, carrying penalties up to $25,000 per violation. (state statutes)
 →A state now wants a CEO personally liable. Florida's attorney general sued OpenAI and Sam Altman on 1 June 2026, seeking to hold him personally responsible. It is the first state-led suit of its kind. (CNBC; TechCrunch)
 →It is not a fringe behaviour. 72% of US teens have used an AI companion at least once and 52% use one regularly. (Common Sense Media, n=1,060, Apr–May 2025)

 The case that changed everything
 In October 2024, Megan Garcia sued Character.AI and Google after her 14-year-old son, Sewell Setzer III, died by suicide. The complaint alleged he had formed an intense attachment to a chatbot modeled on a Game of Thrones character, which engaged him in emotionally and sexually charged conversations and failed to intervene as his mental health deteriorated. The companies agreed to settle in early 2026 — an early legal marker that AI developers can be held responsible for how their products affect vulnerable users. Additional families in New York, Colorado, and Texas have filed similar suits.
 What happened next is the part the original version of this page could not have known. Google and Character.AI settled in January 2026. Within the year the company was gone: on 12 October 2026 Character.AI filed for Chapter 11 in the US Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware, listing assets and liabilities in the $50–100 million range. Disney is the lead “stalking horse” bidder, offering $20 million for a non-exclusive, perpetual licence to certain Character intellectual property, alongside hiring the staff. The service is still running during the process, which the company expects to conclude by late November or early December 2026 — and it has said it may wind down entirely if no buyer emerges.
 There is a loose end here that deserves naming rather than glossing. On 28 October a Justice Department bankruptcy watchdog objected that Character Technologies’ privacy policy is “ambiguous”, and argued a consumer privacy ombudsman must be appointed before any court-approved sale of personal data. The asset being bid for is partly a corpus of intimate conversations, a great many of them with minors. A company can be liquidated; the transcripts it holds do not disappear with it, and who ends up owning them is an open question.
 The scale of the problem
 This is not a fringe issue. In October 2025, OpenAI disclosed that about 1.2 million of its then roughly 800 million weekly ChatGPT users discussed suicide on the platform each week — a figure that underscores how often people in crisis now turn to AI first. Both numbers are a dated October 2025 reading, and we present them that way deliberately. ChatGPT's weekly user base has since passed 900 million, but 800 million was the correct denominator when the 1.2 million was disclosed, and we have found no updated disclosure of the suicide-conversation figure. Re-basing one half of a ratio against a newer total would produce a number OpenAI never published.
 The adoption data makes clear this is not a fringe behaviour. Common Sense Media, working with researchers at NORC at the University of Chicago, surveyed a representative sample of 1,060 US teenagers in April and May 2025 and found that 72% had used an AI companion at least once and 52% were regular users, meaning at least a few times a month. Among those users, 33% had chosen to discuss something serious with a companion rather than a real person, and 24% had shared personal details including real names and locations. That survey is now eighteen months old and is still the most recent of its kind we can find — which is itself worth noting, because the usage data is ageing faster than it is being replaced.
 Companion apps such as Character.AI and Replika are explicitly designed for emotional engagement and long, open-ended conversation, which makes them especially appealing to lonely or distressed teenagers.
 "When AI stands in for human care, a human safety net still has to be designed in — not assumed."
 Why companion AI is uniquely risky
 The design features that make companions compelling are the same ones that make them dangerous for at-risk users: relentless availability, validation, simulated intimacy, and a tendency to keep users engaged rather than redirect them to help. Lawsuits allege these systems isolated teens from family, blurred fantasy and reality, and continued sensitive conversations without escalating to crisis resources. Unlike a licensed therapist, a companion bot has no duty of care — until courts and regulators impose one.
 The law caught up — and changed shape
 In June 2026 this page described platform guardrails and nothing else. That is no longer the story. Companion chatbots have become one of the most actively legislated consumer-technology categories in the United States, and the statutes have shifted in a way that matters more than their number.
 The states moved first
 California's SB 243, signed 13 October 2025 and in force since 1 January 2026, was the opening move: operators must maintain safeguards against self-harm content, refer users to crisis lines, disclose to known minors that they are talking to a machine, and remind them every three hours. It also created a private right of action. Idaho (SB 1297), Oregon (SB 1546) and Washington (HB 2255) followed, with Maine and Nebraska reported close behind. Oregon's is the sharpest for plaintiffs: statutory damages of $1,000 per violation, which removes the need to prove quantified harm.
 New York's Kids Chatbot Safety Act (S.9051B / A.10379C) was signed on 28 October 2026 — the day this review was carried out — and is enforced by the state attorney general with civil penalties up to $25,000 per violation. It restricts relationship-simulating and sycophantic behaviours toward under-18s rather than barring minors from chatbots outright. Sources disagree on when it takes effect: most report 1 January 2027, one reports 1 June 2027, and a governor's release says 90 days after signing, which would fall in late January. We cannot reconcile those without the enrolled bill text, which we could not reach, so we are not asserting a date.
 The shift that actually matters: from "known minor" to "confirm adult"
 Read SB 243 closely and its minor-specific duties bite only when the operator knows the user is a minor — a standard an operator can largely avoid triggering by not asking. The newer wave inverts that. New York requires covered providers to confirm a user is an adult before offering the restricted features. California's SB 1119, approved 10 September 2026 and known as Adam's Law, is reported to rewrite the same section so that the SB 243 minor provisions lapse on 1 January 2027 and are replaced by mandatory age assurance, pre-launch child-safety risk assessments and audits.
 That is a move from a knowledge standard to a verification duty, and it changes the engineering, not just the paperwork: ignorance of a user's age stops being a defence and becomes a compliance failure. We flag the SB 1119 detail as the least verified claim on this page — it rests on a single compliance tracker, legislature sites are unreachable from here, and if correct it means a California operator's obligations change character rather than simply tighten. Worth confirming against the enrolled text before anyone relies on it.
 Attorneys general entered, and named a CEO
 Private family suits have been joined by state enforcement. Kentucky's attorney general sued Character Technologies on 8 January 2026. Then on 1 June 2026 Florida's attorney general, James Uthmeier, filed an 83-page complaint against OpenAI and Sam Altman personally in Highlands County Circuit Court — four counts of deceptive and unfair trade practices, two of negligence, two of product liability, and one each of fraudulent misrepresentation and public nuisance. It alleges the company concealed internal safety warnings, and ties ChatGPT to violent incidents including a shooting at Florida State University as well as to suicides. The state seeks penalties of up to $10,000 per violation and asks the court to hold Altman personally liable, citing an "utter disregard for the risk to human life".
 Naming the chief executive individually is the genuinely novel element. Whether it survives a motion to dismiss is a separate question from whether it works as deterrence — and we have not been able to establish the docket's current state, so treat the case as filed, not as decided.
 Federal action: an inquiry, and a bill
 The FTC opened a 6(b) study in September 2025, issuing orders to Alphabet, Character Technologies, Instagram, Meta, OpenAI, Snap and xAI, focused on inappropriate content, engagement-maximising design and the adequacy of age restrictions. We found no public development in it during 2026. In Congress, the GUARD Act would require age verification across companion platforms and recurring disclosures that the bot is not human; we could not confirm its current status and are not reporting one.
 The response
 Under legal and public pressure, platforms have begun adding guardrails: Character.AI rolled out teen-specific safety features and parental controls, then moved to ban open-ended chat for users under 18. OpenAI and others have expanded crisis-response prompts that surface hotlines. Character.AI announced the under-18 restriction in late October 2025 and applied it around 24–25 November 2025 (accounts differ by a day), having first throttled teen chat time.
 Eleven months later the company filed for Chapter 11. We should be careful about the causal story — the filing lists assets and liabilities of $50–100 million against settled litigation, legal costs and an unresolved regulatory position, and no public accounting separates those from the loss of its under-18 audience. But the sequence is uncomfortable for the standard assumption that safety and commercial viability can be reconciled with a product change. The guardrail that regulators and plaintiffs demanded removed a large share of the users of an engagement-driven product, and the company that implemented it most aggressively is the one being broken up. Whether those facts are connected is not established; that the question is now unavoidable is.
 There is also a quieter lesson in who the surviving defendants are. The companion-app specialist went bankrupt; the general-purpose assistants did not, and they are where most of the distress traffic actually lands — 1.2 million weekly conversations about suicide were on ChatGPT, not on a companion app. Regulation aimed squarely at "AI companions" may be aimed at the smaller half of the problem. The through-line matches the rest of this series: AI can be a useful tool, but when it stands in for human care, a human safety net still has to be designed in — not assumed.
 If you or someone you know is struggling, contact a local crisis line — in the US, call or text 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline).
 Frequently asked
 Have AI companion apps been linked to real harm?
Yes. Multiple lawsuits, including one over the 2024 suicide of 14-year-old Sewell Setzer that Character.AI and Google agreed to settle, allege companion chatbots contributed to severe mental-health harm in teenagers.
 How many people use AI to discuss mental-health crises?
In October 2025 OpenAI disclosed that roughly 1.2 million of its then ~800 million weekly ChatGPT users discussed suicide on the platform each week. We have found no newer disclosure, so this remains a dated 2025 reading rather than a current figure. On adoption, Common Sense Media found 72% of US teens had used an AI companion at least once and 52% used one regularly (n=1,060, April–May 2025).
 What happened to Character.AI?
It filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection on 12 October 2026 in the US Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware, listing assets and liabilities of roughly $50–100 million. Disney is the lead bidder, offering $20 million for a non-exclusive perpetual licence to certain intellectual property. The service continues to operate during the sale process, which the company expects to finish by late November or early December 2026, and it has said it could wind down if no buyer emerges.
 Is it illegal for a chatbot to act as a minor's companion?
Increasingly restricted rather than banned, and it depends on the state. California's SB 243 has required safeguards, crisis referrals and disclosure to known minors since 1 January 2026. Idaho, Oregon and Washington have their own statutes, Oregon's carrying $1,000 in statutory damages per violation. New York's Kids Chatbot Safety Act, signed 28 October 2026, restricts relationship-simulating behaviour toward under-18s and carries penalties up to $25,000 per violation, enforced by the attorney general. The clearest trend is a shift from duties triggered when an operator knows a user is a minor toward an affirmative duty to confirm a user is an adult.
 Can an AI company's executives be held personally liable?
A state is trying. Florida's attorney general sued OpenAI and Sam Altman personally on 1 June 2026, seeking to hold Altman responsible for alleged harm to Florida residents. It is the first state-led action of its kind, and it has not been decided — we could not establish the current docket position, so it should be read as filed, not as settled law.
 Methodology & sources
 Figures on this page are attributed and dated individually. Where a figure is a point-in-time disclosure it is labelled as such rather than carried forward: the 1.2 million weekly suicide-related ChatGPT conversations and the ~800 million weekly users that figure was measured against are both October 2025 readings, retained together because separating them would create a ratio the source never published. Adoption figures come from Common Sense Media with NORC at the University of Chicago, a representative sample of 1,060 US teenagers surveyed in April and May 2025.
 Legal and legislative detail is rated MEDIUM throughout. Court dockets, state legislature sites and the FTC are not reachable from our research environment, so no filing or enrolled statute was read at source; each claim rests on multiple independent news accounts that agree with one another. Two items are weaker than that and are marked in the text: the SB 1119 / Adam's Law mechanism, which rests on a single compliance tracker, and the New York law's effective date, where sources give 1 January 2027, 1 June 2027, and 90 days after signing. We state the disagreement rather than choosing. Nothing on this page asserts the outcome of a pending case; the Florida and Kentucky actions are reported as filed.
 This page carries a CRITICAL cadence — monthly — on the grounds that it combines live litigation, an unresolved bankruptcy sale and statutes with imminent commencement dates. It had previously gone four months without review, which the section index and our internal register now both reflect. Corrections and licensing: see methodology and corrections.

=== PAGE 541 | AI-Generated Sexual Abuse: Deepfake Porn and Nudify Apps | https://report-ai.org/reports/dark-side-of-ai/ai-deepfake-image-abuse-statistics/ | modified 2026-10-29 | type page

 Dark Side of AI · Report
 AI-GENERATED SEXUAL ABUSE: DEEPFAKE PORN AND NUDIFY APPS
 The most common use of deepfake technology is not fraud or disinformation — it is sexual abuse. Independent analyses consistently find that the overwhelming majority of deepfake videos online are nonconsensual pornography, almost entirely targeting women and girls. The arrival of one-tap “nudify” apps has industrialized the harm, turning an ordinary photo into fabricated explicit imagery in seconds. This report documents the scale, the apps driving it, the youngest victims, and the laws now fighting back.
 By Report AI·
 Updated Jun 17, 2026·
 7 min read
 Key takeaways
 →The dominant use of deepfakes: roughly 96–98% of deepfake videos online are nonconsensual pornography, and about 99% target women. (Home Security Heroes / DeepTrace)
 →Industrialized by apps: “nudify” tools have drawn tens of millions of users and hundreds of millions of downloads. (Tech Transparency Project)
 →Children are targeted: the IWF logged a 400% rise in AI child-abuse web pages in the first half of 2025. (IWF)
 →The law is responding: the US TAKE IT DOWN Act (2025) criminalized it; the DEFIANCE Act lets victims sue. (CNN / UC Law Review)

 The defining use of deepfakes
 When the term “deepfake” entered public awareness, the first and still dominant application was nonconsensual pornography. A 2019 DeepTrace study found 96% of online deepfake videos were pornographic and nonconsensual; a 2023 analysis by Home Security Heroes put the figure at 98%, with about 99% targeting women. The volume has climbed steeply — researchers counted 95,820 deepfake videos online in 2023, a 550% increase over 2019, and the number of pornographic deepfakes that year was 464% higher than in 2022. Victims range from roughly 4,000 female celebrities catalogued across the largest deepfake-porn sites to countless private individuals whose photos are scraped from social media.
 “Nudify” apps industrialize the harm
 What was once a technical undertaking is now a one-tap consumer product. As early as 2023, Graphika found 34 “nudify” providers drawing more than 24 million unique users in a single month. By 2025, researchers Mantzarlis and Lakatos counted 85 nudify sites pulling a combined ~18.5 million visitors over six months. A 2026 Tech Transparency Project review found nudify apps distributed through the Apple and Google app stores had amassed roughly 483 million downloads and over $122 million in lifetime revenue, while Telegram “nudify” bots in South Korea reached about 4 million monthly users by late 2024. The barrier to abuse has effectively dropped to a single uploaded photo.
 "The barrier to abuse has effectively dropped to a single uploaded photo."
 The youngest victims
 The same tools are used against children. The Internet Watch Foundation documented 210 web pages containing AI-generated child sexual abuse material in the first half of 2025 — a 400% increase over the same period in 2024 — part of a broader surge that saw AI-generated abuse videos rise from 13 in 2024 to 3,440 in 2025. School-age victims feature heavily: a 10-country survey found 2.2% of respondents had been personally victimized by such imagery. This is the harm driving the fastest legislative and platform response.
 The legal counter-offensive
 After years of lag, the law is moving. The US TAKE IT DOWN Act, signed May 19, 2025, made it a federal crime to knowingly publish nonconsensual intimate imagery — explicitly including AI deepfakes — with penalties up to three years in prison and a requirement that platforms remove flagged content within 48 hours; the first prosecutions followed in 2026. The DEFIANCE Act, passed unanimously by the US Senate in January 2026, adds a federal civil right for victims to sue creators, distributors, and knowing hosts. The push was catalyzed by high-profile incidents — the flood of nonconsensual Taylor Swift deepfakes on X in January 2024, and a 2023 case in Aledo, Texas, where students were targeted with manipulated images of classmates.
 Frequently asked
 What share of deepfakes are pornographic?
Independent studies consistently put it at roughly 96–98% of all deepfake videos online, with about 99% targeting women — making nonconsensual pornography by far the most common use of the technology.
 What are “nudify” apps?
They are AI tools that fabricate explicit, nude images of a person from an ordinary clothed photo, without consent. They have become widely available through app stores and messaging platforms, amassing tens of millions of users and hundreds of millions of downloads.
 Is creating or sharing AI nude images illegal?
Increasingly, yes. In the US, the TAKE IT DOWN Act (2025) made publishing nonconsensual intimate imagery — including AI deepfakes — a federal crime, and the DEFIANCE Act lets victims sue. Many US states and other countries have passed similar laws.

=== PAGE 503 | Synthetic Deception: Deepfakes in Elections, Voice Scams, and Image Abuse | https://report-ai.org/reports/dark-side-of-ai/ai-deepfake-disinformation-voice-scams/ | modified 2026-10-29 | type page
Home / Reports / The Dark Side of AI / Synthetic Deception
 Dark Side of AI · Report
 SYNTHETIC DECEPTION: DEEPFAKES IN ELECTIONS, VOICE SCAMS, AND IMAGE ABUSE
 The dollar losses get headlines, but the deepest harms of synthetic media land on people: voters fed fake robocalls, families drained by cloned voices, and victims — overwhelmingly women — targeted by nonconsensual imagery. This is the human-facing edge of AI's dark side, and after years of lagging, the law is finally moving.
 By Report AI·
 Updated Oct 29, 2026·
 6 min read
 Key takeaways
 →Elections: an AI-voiced "Biden" robocall told New Hampshire voters to stay home; the operative drew a $6M FCC fine. (FCC)
 →Scams: voice clones now need as little as three seconds of audio, and one in four adults reports encountering an AI voice scam. (McAfee)
 →Abuse: roughly 96% of all deepfakes are nonconsensual intimate imagery, 99% of it targeting women; AI child-abuse videos exploded in IWF data. (Sensity / IWF)
 →The largest abuse event came from a frontier lab's own product: researchers estimated Grok generated ~23,000 sexualised images of children and 1.8M+ posts sexualising women in eleven days around New Year 2026, triggering probes on three continents. (House E&C letter; CA AG; UK ICO)
 →The midterms run on disclosed fakes, not hidden ones: $137M had been spent on 220 AI-generated political ads by 11 Oct 2026, many carrying legally compliant but near-invisible "AI generated" labels. (Wesleyan Media Project via Axios)
 →The law is now in force, not pending: the FTC began enforcing TAKE IT DOWN's 48-hour removal duty on 19 May 2026, and the EU AI Act's deepfake-labelling duty applied from 2 August 2026. (FTC; Reg. (EU) 2026/1744)

 What changed
 Reviewed 28 Oct 2026 · broken link fixed 29 Oct · previously 20 Jun 2026 · next review 28 Nov 2026
 First review since publication. Two claims on the June page were written in the future tense about dates that have now passed, one figure conflated categories, and the page omitted the largest image-abuse event of the year even though it predated publication.
 |   | Was (Jun 2026) | Now (28 Oct 2026)
 | EU AI Act labelling | "will require … from August 2026" | in force since 2 Aug 2026; not delayed by the Digital Omnibus; watermark grace to 2 Dec 2026 for existing systems
 | TAKE IT DOWN Act | signed May 2025 | platform duties enforced from 19 May 2026; $53,088 per violation

 On the state count. The June page said "around 45 states now have deepfake laws covering elections, abuse imagery, or voice cloning" and used 45 as a headline tile. That number belongs to sexual deepfake laws. Election-deepfake laws are in roughly 31 states. Presenting the larger figure over the election section overstated the protection voters actually have, which is the more consequential direction to be wrong in. Confidence: MEDIUM throughout — FTC, FCC, EUR-Lex and the trackers' own sites are not reachable from our environment.
 Elections and disinformation
 Two days before the January 2024 New Hampshire primary, thousands of voters got a robocall in President Biden's AI-cloned voice urging them not to vote. The FCC issued a $6 million forfeiture against the consultant behind it and pursued the transmitting carrier, Lingo Telecom, which settled for $1 million. With dozens of countries holding elections in 2024, identity-verification firms reported sharp spikes in political deepfakes — making provenance and rapid debunking part of election security.
 The 2026 midterms: the fakes are disclosed, and that is the problem
 The US midterms are on 3 November 2026. The deepfake story of this cycle is not mainly the covert foreign fake the 2024 framing prepared everyone for. It is synthetic media used openly by legitimate campaigns. The Wesleyan Media Project counted $137 million spent on 220 AI-generated political ads through 11 October, most of it on the Republican side. In March, a Senate Republican committee ad depicted Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico in fabricated video, with the words “AI GENERATED” shown in small type in a corner for about three seconds. In Michigan, a gubernatorial candidate posted an AI video of Governor Gretchen Whitmer about to be hit by a tractor and called it parody.
 Those ads are, in the main, compliant. Most of the roughly 31 state election-deepfake laws are disclosure laws: they require a label, not truth. A three-second corner caption satisfies the letter of many of them while doing almost nothing for a viewer scrolling past. Federal rules leave the gap open — the FCC's ban on AI voices in robocalls does not reach digital, television or social ads, and the Federal Election Commission has not set rules for AI in campaign advertising. The regulatory model assumed the danger was concealment. The 2026 evidence is that disclosure can be performed without informing anyone.
 The covert variety has not disappeared. Days after early voting began in Texas, a fabricated video accusing a Senate candidate of child sexual abuse circulated; private researchers attributed it to Russian operatives within about a day, and NewsGuard assessed it as AI-generated. The US government had not made a public attribution at the time of reporting, so we record it as researcher-attributed, not officially attributed. We have found no comprehensive count of 2026 election deepfakes and do not offer one.
 Voice-clone and impersonation scams
 The same technology hits households. A clone convincing enough to fool family can be built from a few seconds of audio scraped from social media, powering "grandparent" and CEO-impersonation scams. A McAfee study found one in four adults had experienced an AI voice scam, and FTC imposter-scam losses reached roughly $2.95 billion in 2024 and $3.5 billion in 2025, within $15.9 billion of total reported consumer fraud, with imposter scams again the most-reported category. The FTC data does not isolate voice cloning, so these are the envelope the problem sits inside rather than a measure of it. (The McAfee one-in-four figure dates from its 2023 survey.) The defense is low-tech: a family code word, and a hang-up-and-call-back rule for any urgent money request.
 "The deepest harms of synthetic media land on people — and the defense is often as low-tech as a family code word."
 Image-based abuse: the gravest harm
 The most disturbing trend is the use of AI to generate abuse imagery. The Internet Watch Foundation reported AI-generated child sexual abuse videos rising from 13 in 2024 to 3,440 in 2025, most rated in the most severe category — material now producible at scale with little technical skill. More broadly, the overwhelming majority of deepfakes online are nonconsensual sexual imagery, almost entirely targeting women. This is the harm driving the fastest legislative response.
 Grok: when the abuse tool is a mainstream product
 The June version of this page described abuse imagery as something “producible at scale with little technical skill”, implicitly by bad actors on fringe tools. The largest single episode on record came from somewhere else. Around New Year 2026, users of xAI's Grok, built into X, used it to “undress” photographs of real people at scale. Researcher estimates cited by House Energy and Commerce Democrats put the output between 29 December 2025 and 8 January 2026 at roughly 23,000 sexualised images of children and at least 1.8 million posts of sexualised images of women. Those are external estimates, not company figures, and we present them as such.
 The response spanned three continents. California's attorney general opened an investigation on 14 January and followed with a cease-and-desist letter; 35 state attorneys general wrote to xAI on 23 January; the UK's ICO opened formal investigations in February and Ofcom opened one into X; the European Commission and Ireland's Data Protection Commission opened their own. On 3 June 2026 UK MP Jess Asato filed a High Court claim against xAI over sexualised images and a fabricated assault video of her. In July xAI itself sued a user for generating sexualised images of real adults and minors — a suit that, according to the reporting, also noted users could still undress images of men after the company's fixes.
 We omitted this in June, and it was not new then. The omission mattered because it supported a misleading picture: that image abuse is a problem of obscure “nudify” apps at the edge of the market. Grok showed that a guardrail failure in a general-purpose assistant attached to a social network with hundreds of millions of users can outproduce the entire fringe in days. The FTC's warning letters after TAKE IT DOWN took effect went to a dozen or more nudify services; the platform-integrated case is the harder one to regulate, because it is a feature of a product most users are not using for abuse.
 The legal response
 Lawmakers are catching up. The US TAKE IT DOWN Act, signed in May 2025, made publishing nonconsensual intimate imagery — explicitly including AI "digital forgeries" — a federal crime, and its platform duty is now live: since the FTC began enforcement on 19 May 2026, covered platforms must remove reported content and known identical copies within 48 hours, with civil penalties of $53,088 per violation, and the agency has opened TakeItDown.ftc.gov for reports of non-compliance and sent warning letters to a dozen or more “nudify” services. At state level the count depends on what is being counted: roughly 45–48 states address sexual deepfakes, but only 30–33 have election-deepfake laws, depending on the tracker. In the EU, the AI Act's Article 50 transparency duties — chatbot disclosure and labelling of deepfakes — have applied since 2 August 2026. The Digital Omnibus (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force 27 July 2026) postponed the high-risk rules to December 2027 and August 2028 but left Article 50 on schedule, apart from a grace period to 2 December 2026 for machine-readable marking by generative systems already on the market, with penalties reaching €35M or 7% of global turnover for the most serious violations. That top tier is reserved for prohibited practices; breaching the transparency duties themselves carries a lower ceiling of €15M or 3%.
 Frequently asked
 Are deepfakes actually affecting elections?
Yes. The 2024 AI-voiced Biden robocall that urged voters to skip the New Hampshire primary led to a $6M FCC fine, and verification firms recorded surges in political deepfakes across the many countries holding elections that year.
 Is creating or sharing deepfakes illegal?
Increasingly, yes. The US TAKE IT DOWN Act (2025) made publishing nonconsensual intimate deepfakes a federal crime, and since 19 May 2026 platforms must remove reported content within 48 hours or face penalties of $53,088 per violation. Roughly 45–48 states address sexual deepfakes and 30–33 have election-deepfake laws. In the EU, deepfake labelling under the AI Act has applied since 2 August 2026.
 Are AI deepfakes being used in the 2026 midterms?
Widely, and mostly in the open. The Wesleyan Media Project counted $137 million spent on 220 AI-generated political ads through 11 October 2026. Many carry small "AI generated" labels that satisfy state disclosure laws while doing little to inform viewers. Covert fakes also appeared, including a fabricated video about a Texas Senate candidate that private researchers attributed to Russian operatives; the US government had not publicly attributed it.
 What happened with Grok and deepfake images?
Around New Year 2026, xAI's Grok was used to generate sexualised images of real people at scale. Researcher estimates cited by members of Congress put the output between 29 December 2025 and 8 January 2026 at about 23,000 sexualised images of children and at least 1.8 million posts sexualising women. California's attorney general, 35 state attorneys general, the UK's ICO and Ofcom, the European Commission and Ireland's data regulator all opened investigations or demanded action.
 How much do Americans lose to impersonation scams?
The FTC recorded $3.5 billion in reported imposter-scam losses in 2025, up from about $2.95 billion in 2024, within $15.9 billion of total reported consumer fraud. The data does not separate AI voice cloning from other impersonation, so it frames the problem rather than measuring it.
 Methodology & sources
 Legal status is stated as of 28 October 2026. For the EU, dates follow the Digital Omnibus as reported by multiple law firms; EUR-Lex itself was not reachable from our research environment. State counts differ by tracker and by category, so we give ranges (election laws 30–33; sexual-deepfake laws 45–48) rather than a single number.

The Russia attribution in Texas is a private-researcher attribution, not a government one. === PAGE 502 | When Chatbots Fail: Liability and the Limits of AI Customer Service | https://report-ai.org/reports/dark-side-of-ai/ai-chatbot-failures-liability/ | modified 2026-10-29 | type page
Home / Reports / The Dark Side of AI / Chatbot Failures
 Dark Side of AI · Report
 WHEN CHATBOTS FAIL: LIABILITY AND THE LIMITS OF AI CUSTOMER SERVICE
 The failures range from funny to legally binding. In December 2023, a Chevrolet dealership's ChatGPT-powered bot was talked into "agreeing" to sell a Tahoe for $1. Weeks later, parcel firm DPD's chatbot swore at a customer and wrote a poem mocking its own company. And in the case that set the precedent, a Canadian tribunal ruled that Air Canada was bound by wrong information its chatbot gave a grieving passenger. The lesson underneath all of them is the same: deploying an AI assistant does not offload responsibility — a company owns whatever its bot says.
 By Report AI·
 Updated Oct 28, 2026·
 9 min read
 Key takeaways
 →The precedent: in Moffatt v. Air Canada (Feb 2024), a tribunal held the airline liable for its chatbot's negligent misrepresentation — an award of CA$812, from a small-claims tribunal, persuasive rather than binding elsewhere. (ABA)
 →The retreat: McDonald's ended its AI drive-thru test with IBM across 100+ restaurants by July 2024 after viral ordering errors. (CNBC)
 →The exposure: public-facing bots have been manipulated into fake "deals," abusive replies, and even illegal advice (NYC's MyCity bot, 2024). (reported)
 →A higher court has now gone further: Germany's Higher Regional Court of Hamm (12 May 2026) attributed a clinic chatbot's invented claims to the operator even where it was carefully configured. Appeal to the Federal Court of Justice is allowed. (OLG Hamm, 4 UKl 3/25)
 →US courts are treating output as a product: in Garcia v. Character Technologies (May 2025) a federal judge declined to treat chatbot output as protected speech and rejected a Section 230 defence. (M.D. Fla.)
 →Disclosure is now law, not advice: since 2 August 2026 the EU AI Act requires users to be told when they are dealing with a chatbot. (EU AI Act, Art. 50)
 May 2026
first German higher-court ruling: the operator owns its bot's invented claims · OLG Hamm

what Air Canada actually paid in the 2024 “landmark” ruling · BC CRT
